newsitem.title: CANADA: FEATURE-Cirque's newest production opens to crowds and raves.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Cirque's newest production opens to crowds and raves.

text.p: To call it a circus, especially in its latest incarnation, does it a great disservice.

Cirque du Soleil, the internationally acclaimed French Canadian troupe, opened its new production "Quidam" in Toronto last month and the crowds have been near capacity as critics heap praise on its latest effort. But the show, which embarks on a U.S. tour beginning this month, defies easy description.

Is it the greatest show on Earth with its outrageous clowns, juggling and death-defying high wire acts? Is it modern-day burlesque with lithe bodies in exotic costumes intermingling with clowns in comic drag? Is it the Wizard of Oz, mixing comedy and death images, with pointy-headed characters and one with no head at all?

Perhaps all of the above. "Spectacular, breathtaking, amazing -- they're the sort of superlatives you can't help trot out when this circus comes to town," wrote Geoff Chapman, drama critic for the Toronto Star, Canada's largest circulation newspaper.

"Quidam" (pronounced kee-dam) is the ninth production from the phenomenally successful Cirque du Soleil, founded in Montreal a dozen years ago by onetime street performers. The Cirque was forged after a group of fire eaters, jugglers, buskers and stilt walkers -- all part of the High Heels Club, named after their ability to walk on stilts -- staged an outdoor festival to encourage new ideas from a wide collection of Quebec performing artists.

With help from a grant from Quebec's separatist government of the day, which sought to promote French artistry, the idea for a whole new kind of circus was launched. The first production under their now trademark blue and yellow tent drew a capacity crowd of 800.

The Cirque's popularity exploded in Quebec and in Canada but it quickly outgrew its borders. It went on the road to the United States in 1987 and to Europe and Asia beginning in the 1990s, helping it to mushroom into a multinational entertainment success story. The troupe estimates that more than 10 million people have seen its shows and revenues are said to have topped $100 million a year.

Certainly part of its appeal is that it has not forgotten its humble French Canadian roots. It also understands the cachet of its heritage, rarely Anglicizing its name to become a mere "circus" and performing much of the show in French.

Cirque du Soleil is now juggling four productions: Quidam; Alegria, which is performing in Asia; Saltimbanco, which is in Europe, and a permanent production in Las Vegas, a company spokeswoman said. There are plans for more permanent shows, including one at Walt Disney World in Florida beginning in 1998 and one in Berlin.

Quidam, produced by the company's veteran director, Franco Dragone, is seen by critics as its darkest and most mysterious production to date. Dragone says the show is his most scripted ever and is intended to be about people finding their place in the world as the century draws to a close. "This show highlights our frailties and our anguish in the face of the new millennium that lies before us," his production notes say.

Quidam is Latin for the anonymous passerby and the show is filled with strange, comical and sometimes scary figures that entertain a young girl after her parents magically fly away on their parlour room seats. While the girl sings in haunting, etheral tones accompanied by the live musical score, the parents are seemingly banished for most of the production for ignoring the fantastic world around them.

The cast of 50 at the opening was international in scope with performers from Russia, China, France and Canada. Ages of the cast ranged from 11 to 45. One of the more arresting acts was performed by Isabelle Vaudelle, who conducted an erotic mid-air contortionist act slithering down a blazing column of red fabric from the tent's roof.

Another standout was an act by four young Chinese girls in costumes reminiscent of the Tin Man who tossed wooden spools while leaping theatrically around the stage. Their act with the so-called Diablo, a Chinese yo yo, won a gold medal at the 1995 Festival du Cirque de Demain in Paris.

The show was also a high-tech production, although not obtrusively so. It was performed under an enormous tent planted on the shores of Lake Ontario with a huge revolving stage. An aerial conveyor with ten computer-guided trolleys was used to transport performers across the stage in their high wire acts.

Quidam will begin its U.S. tour in Santa Monica, California, on Sept. 25 before hitting Orange County, San Francisco and San Jose. It will remain in the United States into 1998, reaching the East Coast with its show in New York on April 8, 1998.
